title: Collective hallucinations and inefficient markets: The British Railway Mania of the 1840s
claim: Investors in the 1840s had public traffic data showing demand could not support the lines being financed; share prices implied railway revenues of about 60 million pounds by 1850-52 against about 6 million in 1845, and actual 1852 revenue was about 15 million.
changes: Back out the revenue that current AI capex and valuations imply for a target year and compare it with the observable usage trend each quarter; flag the book when implied revenue runs more than about 2x the trend line.
verified: Fetched the PDF from Odlyzko's university page; figures read from the main text.

title: Internet growth: Myth and reality, use and abuse
claim: The claim that internet traffic doubled every three or four months (700 to 1,500 percent a year), used to justify the fiber build, was false; US backbone traffic was about doubling annually.
changes: Treat any vendor or company demand-growth figure (tokens, compute hours) as unverified until it is reconciled with an independent measurement, and size capex bets on the independent series.
verified: Fetched the PDF from Odlyzko's university page; data in it runs to February 2001.

title: Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital: The Dynamics of Bubbles and Golden Ages
claim: Each of five technological revolutions since the 1770s was installed by financial capital running ahead of production capital, through a frenzy that decoupled finance from the technology's real capabilities, before a crash and a slower deployment phase.
changes: Add a phase tag to the desk view (installation, frenzy, turning point, deployment) with written criteria, and require the sizing call to state which phase it assumes.
verified: Publisher listing at Edward Elgar; EH.net review describing the phase sequence; Wikipedia entry.

title: Railroaded: The Transcontinentals and the Making of Modern America
claim: The transcontinental railroads were the first corporate giants, and their efforts to profit from growing debt and public support helped cause severe economic panics and new forms of political corruption.
changes: For each of the nine names, track how much of the buildout is funded by debt or public subsidy that sits off the parent's income statement, and treat rising reliance on it as a risk signal rather than a sign of strength.
verified: Fetched Stanford History department publication page (year, publisher, argument).

title: Devil Take the Hindmost: A History of Financial Speculation
claim: A history of speculation from the 1630s tulip episode through the South Sea Bubble, the 1840s railway mania, the 1920s and Japan's bubble economy, arguing speculative behaviour has changed less than people expect.
changes: Keep a written list of past-mania signatures (new issuance of vehicles that only own other vehicles, retail leverage, vendor financing) and score the current cycle against it once a quarter.
verified: Fetched the author's book page (year, scope).

title: The Price of Time: The Real Story of Interest
who: Edward Chancellor (Atlantic Monthly Press; Grove paperback 2026)
claim: Argues that rates held at historic lows after 2008 fed asset bubbles, weak productivity and excessive risk-taking by yield-starved investors, because interest is the price that allocates capital across time.
changes: When real rates rise, rerun the book's valuation and credit screens on the assumption that projects financed at zero-rate hurdle rates are the first to fail, and watch the private credit marks on those vintages.
verified: Fetched Grove Atlantic book page (dates, argument).

title: Boom and Bust: A Global History of Financial Bubbles
who: William Quinn and John D. Turner (Cambridge University Press)
claim: Bubbles over 300 years needed three sides at once (marketability of assets, cheap money and credit, speculative buying) plus a spark from new technology or government policy.
changes: Build a three-gauge bubble monitor (ease of trading the asset, credit availability, momentum-driven flows) and only raise bubble risk in the sizing engine when all three read high at once.
verified: IMF Finance and Development review fetched (triangle and spark); Cambridge chapter PDF located.

title: The Great Crash, 1929
claim: Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation, launched in December 1928, stacked Shenandoah and then Blue Ridge inside itself, funded largely with 6 percent convertible preference stock, and its shares later fell 97 percent from the 1929 high to 4 3/8.
changes: When vehicles that own other vehicles (SPVs, JV data-center holdcos, funds of BDCs) proliferate, compute the look-through leverage to the bottom asset and size exposure off that number, not the top-level ratio.
verified: Fetched a summary page that cites The Great Crash 1929 as its source; the book is listed in the Library of America Galbraith volume (storyoftheweek.loa.org).

title: The Merchant of Power: Sam Insull, Thomas Edison, and the Creation of the Modern Metropolis
claim: Insull built a roughly 4 billion dollar pyramid of highly leveraged utility holding companies (he chaired 65 boards) that unravelled in 1932 when demand fell, leading Congress to pass the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935.
changes: For power and data-center names financed through layered holdcos, stress test a 10 to 20 percent fall in contracted demand and check whether the top entity's equity survives the debt service of the layers below.
verified: Publishers Weekly listing for the book; EBSCO Research Starter on the Insull utilities collapse fetched for the figures.

title: Broadbandits: Inside the $750 Billion Telecom Heist
claim: WorldCom, Qwest, Lucent and Global Crossing spent heavily on fiber for broadband customers who did not arrive in time; when the bubble burst about 750 billion dollars of wealth disappeared and some 600,000 jobs were lost, while insiders sold stock.
changes: Pair every capex-heavy name with its insider selling and its supplier-financing disclosures in the filings desk, and treat heavy insider sales during peak capex guidance as a downgrade trigger.
verified: getAbstract summary page fetched (publisher, year, figures); Wiley product page located.

title: Historical construction costs of global nuclear power reactors
who: Jessica Lovering, Arthur Yip, Ted Nordhaus (Energy Policy vol. 91)
claim: Using overnight construction costs for 349 reactors in seven countries (about 58 percent of reactors ever built), the authors find the rapid US cost escalation was not universal; some countries saw mild escalation or outright declines.
changes: When pricing firm-power and nuclear supply-chain names, model cost overruns by country and builder experience (serial builds versus first-of-a-kind) instead of applying one US-style escalation rate; also read the 2016 Koomey et al. reply that disputes the data.
verified: Fetched RePEc abstract page; search also surfaced the published reply critiquing it.

title: The Grid: The Fraying Wires Between Americans and Our Energy Future
claim: A cultural and technical history of the US electric grid arguing it was built for large central plants and steady demand and is poorly suited to the variable supply and new loads now being added to it.
changes: Track interconnection queue times and transmission approvals as a leading indicator for data-center capacity coming online, and treat chip supply as secondary when those times lengthen.
verified: Publishers Weekly listing and multiple library catalog records confirm title, author, publisher and year.

title: How the World Really Works
claim: Modern life rests on four materials (ammonia, cement, steel, plastics) that depend on fossil energy; for example Germany's fossil share of primary energy fell only from 84 to 78 percent after about 400 billion dollars on solar and wind.
changes: Do not let energy-transition timelines reduce the oil-shock tail budget; size it on the assumption that hydrocarbon dependence persists for the life of the book.
verified: Fetched Reason review dated 2022-05-25 (publisher, figures).

title: Crude Volatility: The History and the Future of Boom-Bust Oil Prices
claim: Oil prices were stable only when a controller held spare capacity (Standard Oil, the Texas Railroad Commission, then OPEC); with no reliable swing producer, swings like 147.27 dollars in July 2008 to 30.28 dollars that December become the norm.
changes: Make OPEC+ effective spare capacity an explicit input to the oil-shock hedge: when spare capacity is thin, raise the size of the standing upside oil protection.
verified: Fetched London Review of Books review (argument, price figures); Columbia University Press blog and library records confirm publication.

title: The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money, and Power

changes: Keep a dated list of every major supply disruption in the book (1956 Suez, 1973, 1979, 1990) with size and duration, and calibrate the oil-shock scenario to the 75th percentile of that list rather than the most recent episode.

title: The New Map: Energy, Climate, and the Clash of Nations

title: Bernoulli's Fallacy: Statistical Illogic and the Crisis of Modern Science

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
who: David H. Bailey and Marcos Lopez de Prado (Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5))
claim: Testing many strategy variants and reporting the best inflates the Sharpe ratio; the deflated Sharpe ratio corrects for the number of trials and for non-normal returns.

title: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
claim: Top forecasters in the Good Judgment Project were about 30 percent more accurate than intelligence analysts with access to classified data, mainly through frequent small updates and teamwork.

title: Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts
